## Channel Islands

The **Channel Islands** are a chain of eight islands located off the southern coast of California in the Pacific Ocean. They are known for their stunning natural beauty, ecological richness, and deep cultural history.

### The Eight Channel Islands (North to South)

1.  **San Miguel Island**

2.  **Santa Rosa Island**

3.  Santa Cruz Island

4.  Anacapa Island

5.  Santa Barbara Island

6.  San Nicolas Island

7.  San Clemente Island

8.  Santa Catalina Island

Below we will only consider the two bolded islands: SMI and SRI

### [Channel Islands National Park](https://www.nps.gov/chis/index.htm)

-   Includes **five islands**: *San Miguel*, *Santa Rosa*, *Santa Cruz*, *Anacapa*, and *Santa Barbara*.
-   Sometimes called the "Galápagos of North America" for its rich biodiversity and many **endemic species**.
-   Accessible only by *boat or small plane*.
-   Ideal for hiking, kayaking, camping, and wildlife observation.

### Cultural and Historical Significance

-   Originally inhabited by [**Chumash** and **Tongva**](https://www.nps.gov/chis/learn/historyculture/nativeinhabitants.htm#:~:text=With%20a%20current%20population%20nearly,organized%20Chumash%20tribal%20groups%20exist) indigenious groups for thousands of years.
-   Home to important archaeological and cultural heritage sites.

## Island Fox (*Urocyon littoralis*)

The **island fox** is a small, charismatic canid species *endemic* to six of the eight *Channel Islands* off the coast of southern California. It's one of the best examples of **island dwarfism**, having evolved from the mainland gray fox (*Urocyon cinereoargenteus*) to become significantly smaller.

In the **1990s**, several island fox populations faced **near extinction** due to golden eagle predation, canine distemper virus, and habitat degradation. The island fox was listed as endangered in 2004. Recovery efforts of the island fox included removal of golden eagles, vaccination and captive breeding programs, reintroduction of native bald eagles, and habitat restoration.

## Data and Prep {#intro}


The data provided is part of an ongoing longitudinal study of island foxes from 2014 to 2016 of trap monitoring. This resulted in collection of 4,975 recorded trap observations, which may have contained a fox or not. Other information collected were Sex, Age Class, Weight, Body Condition, Reproductive Status, and Vaccinations. Information on the data collected can be found in the [Databook](https://github.com/mludkov/UCSB_Data_Day_2026/blob/gh-pages/data_for_datathon_2014_2016.csv).


### Loading Packages

The `tidyverse` suite is a collection of data analysis packages:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

### Loading Data

We will load the data into the R workspace using the `read_csv` function:

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Need to modify to load the file from the location where you downloaded it
df <- read_csv(here::here("data_for_datathon_2014_2016.csv")) # Loads the Data Set into the object df
```

### Cleaning Data

#### Renaming Categories

Looking at the [Codebook](https://github.com/mludkov/UCSB_Data_Day_2026/blob/gh-pages/IslandFoxes_codebook.pdf), the variables `Vaccinations`, `ReproductiveStatus` and `BodyCondition` are coded in interesting ways. In `Vaccinations`, missing values (`NA`) are considered as not vaccinated; therefore, changing the missing to "NV" will ensure that they are correctly classified. In `ReproductiveStatus`, the missing values (`NA`) indicate unknown reproductive status. In `BodyCondition`, the numerical values 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, represent a condition. To make the condition easier, we will convert them to the categories. Run the code below to alter them:

```{r}
df <- df |> mutate( # Will change the variables in the df data set
    Vaccinations = case_when(is.na(Vaccinations) ~ "NV", .default = Vaccinations), # Reclassifies Missing Data in Vaccination as "N" per code book.
    ReproductiveStatus = case_when(is.na(ReproductiveStatus) ~ "UN", .default = ReproductiveStatus), # Reclassifies Missing Data in Vaccination as "N" per code book.
    BodyCondition = case_when( # Begins to modify BodyCondition
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "1" ~ "emaciated", # Changes 1 to emaciated
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "2" ~ "thin", # Changes 2 to thin
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "3" ~ "healthy wild", # Changes 3 to healthy wild 
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "4" ~ "extra fat reserves", # Changes 4 to Extra Fat Reserve
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "5" ~ "extreme fat reserves" # Changes 5 to Extreme Fat Reserves
        )
    )
```

#### Missing Values

Several variables in the data set may be missing. Using the `summary()`, we can determine which variables have missing values by looking at the "NA's" category.

```{r}
summary(df)
```


We notice that the variables `AgeClass`, `Weight`, and `BodyCondition` have missing values. **For this analysis, we will remove the missing values (`NA`).**

```{r}
df <- drop_na(df, AgeClass, Weight, BodyCondition) # Removes the missing values (NA) using the variables AgeClass, Weight, and BodyCondition
```

**After cleaning the data, this should result in 1,967 recorded foxes!** This is the dataset that we will be using for the rest of this activity.

```{r}
nrow(df)
```

## Part I: {#part1}
### Fox Weight Analysis {#fox-weight}

Imagine you're a field biologist tracking animal health across the remote Santa Rosa and San Miguel Islands. You’ve noticed that some animals seem heavier in certain years—but is it just your imagination, or is there a real trend?

The `Weght` variable contains information of the Fox's weight in kilograms. Let's start by calculating the mean weight and standard deviation of weight using `mean()` and `sd()` functions:

```{r}
mean_weight<-mean(df$Weight)
sd_weight<-sd(df$Weight)
mean_weight
sd_weight #printing the values
```
We see that mean weight of a fox is about 1.9 kg (which is about 4 pounds) with standard deviation about .41 kg.

We use the `table()` and `prop.table()` functions to get the frequencies and proportions for the `Sex`.

```{r}
count_df <- table(df$Sex) # Using the 'Sex' variable from the `df` data set, we count the frequencies of each category with the table function and storing it in rs_df.
count_df # Printing out the contents of "rs_df"
```

Using the `table()` function, we can see that there were 923 female and 1044 male Foxes captured.

```{r}
prop.table(count_df) # Computing the Proportions of "rs_df"
```

The `prop.table()` function shows the respective percentages: there are slightly more male Foxes (about 53%) vs. female Foxes (about 47%).

We can visualize the data using the `ggplot` functions. Namely we build a bar plot that shows those above counts visually (with more Male than Female foxes):

```{r}
ggplot(df) + # Setting up the data to create a plot.
  geom_bar(aes(Sex)) + # Creating a bar chart based on the variable "ReproductiveStatus" 
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 14))
```


### Weight vs Sex

Let's visualize the variable `Weight` and `Sex` with a boxplot using `ggplot`:

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(x = Sex, y = Weight)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Boxplot of Weight by Sex",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Weight"
  ) + theme_minimal()
```
From the box plot we see that male Foxs tend to be slightly *heavier* than female Foxes.

We can use `group_by()` function to separate male from female population and calculate means and standard deviations separately:

```{r}
weight_summary <- df %>%
  group_by(Sex) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_weight = mean(Weight),
    sd_weight = sd(Weight),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
weight_summary

```
This table confirms that male Foxes are slightly heavier, with mean weight of about 1.99 kg, than female Foxes, whose mean weight is about 1.88 kg. Standard deviations  are also slightly higher for male Foxes.

#### Weight vs Sex over time

To see weight vs sex trend over time we can use `group_by()` and `ggplot` functions again:

```{r}
weight_summary_yearly <- df %>%
  group_by(Sex, SamplingYear) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_weight = mean(Weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_weight = sd(Weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) #group the data by Sex and Year and calculate mean and standard deviation of weight
weight_summary_yearly
```
From the table we see a downward trend in weight for both females and males across years. Let's plot it on the graph:

```{r}
ggplot(weight_summary_yearly, aes(x = SamplingYear, y = mean_weight)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_weight - sd_weight,
                    ymax = mean_weight + sd_weight), width = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Sex) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Weight by Year and Sex",
    y = "Mean Weight",
    x = "Year"
  )
```
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
#### Weight vs Sex over time by Island

Here is a first question for you to answer: do the foxes on different islands have the same weight? Is there an island where the foxes are **significantly** heavier than others? To conduct such analysis, you can filter by different `Islands`:

```{r}
#Santa Rosa Fox population 

SR_df<-filter(df,Island=="SRI")

#San Miguel Fox population
SM_df<-filter(df,Island=="SMI")

```
:::

### Questions to Try Out

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}

Do vaccinated foxes have a different weight compared to unvaccinated ones? To answer this, study the relationship between `Weight` and `Vaccinations`
:::

The dataset has a variable called `BodyCondition`. What proportion of foxes are well nourished? Do some islands have a larger proportion of "fat" foxes than others? How does `BodyCondition` connect with `Weight`? For the latter, you could look into scatter plots.

### Fox Reproductive Status Analysis {#fox-rs}

The `ReproductiveStatus` variable contains information of the Fox's reproductive status when captures. This data is recorded as "N" (Not actively reproductive), "L" (Lactating), "SL" (Signs of Lactating), and "TD" (Testes Distended).

We will use the `table()` and `prop.table()` function to get the frequencies and proportions for the `ReproductiveStatus`.

```{r}
rs_df <- table(df$ReproductiveStatus) # Using the 'ReproductiveStatus' variable from the `df` data set, we count the frequencies of each category with the table function and storing it in rs_df.
rs_df # Printing out the contents of "rs_df"
```

Using the `table()` function, we can see that there are 3 common reproductive statuses by Fox: "L" at 18, "SL" at 244, "TD" at 1030, and "UN" at 675.

```{r}
prop.table(rs_df) # Computing the Proportions of "rs_df"
```

Using the `prop.table()` function, we can see that that the most common status is "TD" at 52.4% and the least common is "L" at the 0.9%. Both "SL" and "UN" represent 12.4% and 34.3% of the data, respectively. In barplot format we have:

```{r}
ggplot(df) + # Setting up the data to create a plot.
  geom_bar(aes(ReproductiveStatus)) # Creating a bar chart based on the variable "ReproductiveStatus"
```


#### Sex and Reproductive Status

Let's compare the frequencies between the variables `Sex` and `Reproductive Status`. We will be using the same `table()` function:

```{r}
xy_df <- table(df$ReproductiveStatus, df$Sex)
# Use the variables "ReproductiveStatus" and "Sex" from the "df" data set
# Use the table function to compute the crosstabs
# Store the results in the xy_df object

xy_df # Print results out
```

The results show that certain categorical combinations between `ReproductiveStatus` and `Sex` are 0, which is to be expected. The category "UN" is found in both Male and Female foxes. Looking at Female foxes, The most common type is "UN", followed by "SL". For Male foxes, the most common type was "TD".

Let's find the proportions for each the combination of the variables using the `prop.table()` function.

```{r}
prop.table(xy_df)
```

We can see that 52.4% of the data are Male and "TD" foxes, 33.6% of the data are Female and "UN" foxes, and 12.4% of the data are Female and "SL" foxes. To visualize how the variable `ReproductiveStatus` and `Sex` related to each other we use a stacked bar plot:

```{r}
ggplot(df) +
  geom_bar(aes(Sex, fill = ReproductiveStatus)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 14))
```

The plot indicate which categories are most dominant in each sex. We can see that the most dominant reproductive status in Male foxes is testes distended. For Female foxes, we can see that the most common reproductive status is Unknown.

### Challenges

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
#### Age Class

How does `ReproductiveStatus` relate to `AgeClass` (how old is the fox), to `Vaccinations`, and to `Capture Type`.
:::

How many skunks were caught each year? Are there more skunks on some island than others? (Look at `TrapResult`. Note that some skunks were caught but escaped, see the different possible values of this field!)

Analyze how often do the traps work (expressed as a success percentage). Namely, which Island and which Years yield the most foxes?
:::




## Part 2: For More Advanced Participants {#part2}

### Tracking Foxes

Each fox gets a unique Pit Tag.  This `Pittag` field allows to track a specific fox across time. For example, let's consider fox with tag  989001000124022. It shows up in the following records:

```{r}
library(knitr)
knitr::kable(df[which(df$Pittag==989001000124022),])
```


Looking at these records, we can see that it is a Female fox on Santa Rosa Island that was observed 3 times during the same week in August 2016. The first capture it was tagged (`CaptureType` = New) and then it was re-tagged twice more. 

### Questions to Try Out

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
#### Tagging Statistics
How many different foxes have been tagged? If you look at `CaptureType' you can also analyze how many foxes have been observed multiple times. What fraction of foxes were observed just once? How many unique foxes are on each of the two islands?

:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
#### Fox Life Story

Find an ``interesting'' fox that has been observed across a lengthy interval of time (multiple months and years). Investigate its record and write down a story about the life of this fox. For example: how did its weight, reproductive  and vaccination status evolve over time? The aim of this Challenge is to convert the data/numbers into a verbal narrative/words. 
:::

#### Time Series

While above we considered the general **population** trends of how foxes are across the years, this evidence is not so conclusive because potentially it is about different foxes. A stronger analysis would directly track the same fox across time. *Time series*, where we put the date (in our case `TrapDate`) on the x-axis and the numeric variable of interest (say `Weight`) on the y-axis serve this purpose. To be interesting however, the time span needs to be long enough -- it is not so interesting to make a time series for fox 989001000124022 that was only ever observed over a single week in 2016. 

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
#### Fox Time Series
Find foxes that are observed across multiple months/years and create time series plots for them. Report how your findings align or differ from the population-analysis we did in the Introduction. 

:::
